display_title: Training networks with multiplicative input noise: interesting but with questions

content.title: Training networks with multiplicative input noise: interesting but with questions
content.review:
In this paper, a so-called explainable adversarial learning approach is proposed. It is shown that the use of multiplicative input noise can enhance the robustness of neural networks. My detailed comments are as below. 

1) The definition of 'Explainable' is not convinced. The authors claimed that "the model not only finds the right prediction but also the right explanation. Noise inculcates this explainable behavior by discovering some knowledge about the input/output distribution during training." The distribution of the learnt noise is not surprising since by minimizing the training loss, the noise should reflect the example pattern. I am not convinced about the name 'explainable adversarial learning'.

2) In ExL (Algorithm 1), why not consider the affine transformation X N_1 + N_2, where both N_1 and N_2 are learnt from the training process? Is this better than X N_1? What is the rationale behind using universal noise pattern over different minibatches. 

3) The proposed ExL framework is quite similar to training over perturbed examples. Here the perturbation is given by X \times N.  It is expected that ExL will not outperform adversarial training but will outperform the plain training in robustness. From this perspective, I feel that the results are not very impressive. 

4) The study on Sec. 2.3 via PCA is nice and Figure 3 is informative. 

5) Since the proposed ExL training framework is scaled to large datasets, it is better to cover more experiments, e.g., ImageNet.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to Reviewer3 (Part1)
content.comment:
1)	The term ‘explainable’ was used in the context that noise (on account of being trained with the model) discovers some knowledge about the input/output distribution. We did not mean to confuse with interpretability of a network’s decision making procedure or what it sees in the input to predict a confident output. Thank you for pointing this out. We will change the title of the paper to “Implicit Generative Modeling of Random Noise during Training for Adversarial Robustness” and replace the Explainable learning (ExL) with noise-based adversarial learning (AdL) in the paper. 

a.	We understand your comment “it is not surprising since by minimizing the training loss, the noise should reflect the example pattern”.  There has been past works, where random noise or perturbation have been added to images during training, that results in better regularization effect and in turns improves a model’s generalization capability [R1]. Such works, however, do not result in adversarial robustness [R2]. Our partial generative modeling of input level noise during discriminative training is a very novel approach. Because of this implicit generative property, we used the term ‘explainable’. However, we understand it might confuse the readers and hence will change it. To the best of our knowledge, there has been no prior works of using a strategy of training the input-level noise and getting better robustness.
[R1] Fawzi, Alhussein, Seyed-Mohsen Moosavi-Dezfooli, and Pascal Frossard. "Robustness of classifiers: from adversarial to random noise." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. 2016.
[R2] Goodfellow, Ian J, Shlens, Jonathon, and Szegedy, Christian. Explaining and harnessing adversarial examples. In Proc. ICLR, 2015.

2)	To clarify, we have shown in Fig. 2 the effect of using additive (X+N) vs. multiplicative noise (X*N). X+N also yields adversarial robustness as X*N. But X*N training gives test accuracy comparable to that of the standard SGD training method (without noise). If we understand the reviewer’s concern correctly, using two different noise templates i.e. X*(N_1+N_2) instead of (X*N_1) is equivalent to effectively adding more noise templates during training. For instance, for a batch-size of 64, with X*N, we learn 64 noise templates (N) in each iteration of training. Having X* (N_1 +N_2), where each N_1 and N_2 has 64 templates, we will learn 128 templates during training the model. Training has to be carefully fine-tuned(with proper learning rate) to ensure that accuracies do not drop. We will still get adversarial robustness even in this case. Adding more noise templates to learn will slow down the overall learning though (more epochs to reach baseline accuracy comparable to standard SGD).

a.	Rationale for using the same noise templates during training: Since we are training the noise, we need to reuse the noise maps across different mini-batches. We want to make sure that the characteristics of noise learnt in 1st iteration are preserved and passed onto the 2nd iteration of training. This will help the noise, fed to the network with the input (X*N), to enable the overall loss minimization procedure during training. If we introduce new N for each iteration, there will not be any learning of noise. This is equivalent to introducing randomly perturbation every iteration and the noise will not inherit any characteristics.

content.title: Response to Reviewer3 (Part2)
content.comment:
3)	Training over perturbed examples is very much different from our approach. Perturbing examples during training is a way of making the network robust to external perturbations (different from adversarial perturbation). This helps in improving a network’s generalization capability. However, as shown in [R1, R2], using random noise during training does not help adversarial robustness. To clarify, in our case, the input noise (randomly initialized at the beginning) is gradually learnt during the training procedure. This in turn might have some regularization effect that can be seen from the loss smoothening curves in Fig. 5. But, the fact that it improves adversarial robustness is not trivial. 

a.	Our approach while not being able to beat PGD adversarial training for whitebox attack scenarios, is able to come close (and in some cases yield better accuracy) to ensemble adversarial training for black-box attack accuracy as shown in Table 2/1 (Compare ExL and SGD_ens results, illustration shown below). In fact, ExL achieves better whitebox accuracy than SGD_ens showing that even some white-box perturbations are inherited in this implicit noise modeling procedure. Such adversarial robustness cannot be attained with a setup of training over perturbed examples. 
Scenario|Clean|Min BB    |      PGD-7                  PGD-20 |      PGD-7       PGD-20|
                   ExL     |87.1| 81/76/67| 80.1/75.7/66.4    80/74.8/61|   39.1/29.2/23      -    |
          	 SGDens |86.3|81/77/68| 80.9/75.1/67.1   80.2/74.4/63|   0.8/-/- -              -    |

[R1] Fawzi, Alhussein, Seyed-Mohsen Moosavi-Dezfooli, and Pascal Frossard. "Robustness of classifiers: from adversarial to random noise." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. 2016.
[R2] Goodfellow, Ian J, Shlens, Jonathon, and Szegedy, Christian. Explaining and harnessing adversarial examples. In Proc. ICLR, 2015.

4)	Thank you so much for your assessment on the PCA results. 

5)	It is true that ExL can be scaled to larger training datasets. Since, our approach requires a model to be trained from scratch with the noise, we chose smaller yet benchmark datasets. We are planning to include (in the Appendix) the ImageNet results and compare four scenarios (including ensemble adversarial training) of SGD, EXL, SGD_ens, ExL_ens. We would like to note that PGD adversarial training cannot be scaled to large datasets like ImageNet, since we need to create PGD adversaries (with 7 or 20 steps) in order to  create worthy adversaries. Parsing a large model to create PGD adversaries for 1 million images results in training challenges. This has been acknowledged in the original paper by Madry et. al who proposed PGD. Hence, we cannot compare all 6 scenarios as detailed in table 1, 2 of the paper for cifar10/100, MNIST.
a.	A recent work [R1] has demonstrated a novel training method called adversarial logit pairing (ALP) that achieves strong defense against PGD whitebox attacks. We have combined ExL with ALP and have seen improved robustness as compared to only ALP for MNIST and SVHN datasets (used in [R1]). We have not yet scaled the ExL+ ALP method to ImageNet. The ALP results can be included in the paper or Appendix (in case the reviewer deems it necessary).
[R1] Kannan, Harini, Alexey Kurakin, and Ian Goodfellow. "Adversarial Logit Pairing." arXiv preprint arXiv:1803.06373(2018).

Finally, we would like to bring the novelty of our approach to the reviewer’s attention: while it is intuitive that noise will enhance robustness, random noise as employed in training over perturbed examples (where perturbations are not adversarial perturbations) will not give any adversarial robustness. In most adversarial works till now, a model’s resistance to both white-box and black-box attacks is improved with adversarial training. We show that we can actually make a model resistant with just noise modeling (not just adding random noise, but training it). Combining noise modeling with adversarial training furthers this robustness.

display_title: Trained multiplicative noise improves robustness to adversarial attacks

content.title: Trained multiplicative noise improves robustness to adversarial attacks
content.review:
This paper includes multiplicative noise N in training data, such that it trains a model on X\timesN.  The model then trains on both model parameters theta and on the noise itself in an effort to achieve adversarial robustness

Quality
- The empirical results appear sound, which suggest that multiplicative trained noise is a sensible approach
- The writing that leads up to these results is in my opinion problematically vague, as it makes a variety of loose claims and theoretical connections and uses imprecise language.  This results in scientific imprecision, which I detail below in "clarity".
- Some key choices are unsupported.  For example, the choice of fixing noise across batch (as in, there are k noise maps N that are reused across each minibatch) is unclear.  Certainly if you want to train these noise maps, some reuse is required, but the  given sentence "since we want to learn the noise, we use the same k noise templates across all mini-batches..." does not explain this critical choice.
- What does it mean to train a noise map?  I know what it means mechanically, but there is a vague set of explanations that do not leave an empirical or theoretical understanding of why this is a sensible choice.  Connecting this to similarly ill-defined comments on "excessive linearity" or "off manifold" deepen this issue.

Clarity
- The mechanics of the algorithm are sufficiently clear, but the interpretation is deemed highly vague, such that the result is a rather simple algorithm that is wrapped up with loose and unclear explanations.  Some examples are below:
- critical terms are introduced without technical explanation.  For example, "model viability" is introduced in \emph{} as the key questoin in the third paragraph of the introduction.  However, after reading this sentence several times, I don't know what this question is trying to ask.  Is it just "we seek to improve robustness to adversarial attacks"?  Is "such out-of-sample data" meant to point to "off manifold" points?  Other terms like "inculcates", "off manifold", "inherits", "right prediction vs right explanation", etc. add to this issue.
- On that point, the term "off manifold" is used often but is highly vague.  We all know what this means colloquially, but if you want to make a scientific point about it, there needs to be rigor applied to this definition.
- The likelihood perspective (section 2.2) is not rigorous.  These distributions are undefined to a problematic extent.  For example, p(Y|X,\theta) is clear enough, but then what is p(Y|X,A,\theta)?  I understand A is the adversarial inputs, but what *specifically* is this model?  How *specifically* does A represent the adversarial inputs?  Absent this level of definition and detail on this and other points, the likelihood section is deemed highly vague. 

Originality and Significance
- At a basic level, this manuscript offers multiplicative and trained noise maps.  That is a meaningful (albeit small) contribution.  The results are rigorous enough to make it interesting in its own right, but the remainder of the choices are justified via vague language rather than rigorous empiricism.  This limits the perceived significance.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

replying_to: Replying to Trained multiplicative noise improves robustness to adversarial attacks

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2 (Part1)
content.comment:
Clarity related response:
1)	Critical terms are introduced without technical explanation. 

a.	We have used off-manifold points, out-of-sample-data synonymously to refer to adversarial data points. We will clarify this in the manuscript and stick to using out-of-sample data throughout the paper to avoid any confusion.

b.	Regarding use of model viability, we specifically asked this question: ‘Can we improve the viability of the model to generalize better on such out-of-sample-data?’ By viability we imply the dictionary meaning ‘ability to work successfully’. In neural networks, a model’s generalization capability is what allows it to perform prediction and hence work successfully. Since models fail under adversarial attacks, this means that a model is not able to generalize well on such unseen adversarial data. Hence, we framed the question this way to point out the fact that, is there a way to make a model give accurate prediction (that in turn implies improved generalization capability) on out-of-sample data (referring to adversarial data). 

c.	The words ‘inherit’ and ‘inculcates’ have been used to imply that ExL noise based training does improve the robustness of a network to adversarial instances, by enabling the noise to implicitly account or incorporate adversarial data points in the training procedure. The difference between standard SGD training and ExL is the inclusion of noise at the input that is also learnt during the training procedure. We hypothesized that such implicit generative behavior helps a model to incorporate out-of-sample data (which is adversarial data) in the noise learnt which in turn causes the model to become robust to adversarial attacks. 

For instance, we have use ‘inherit’ in phrases: ‘noise templates inherit characteristics from the entire training dataset’ in Sec. 2.1, ‘Since $X$ inherits only the on-manifold data points’ in Sec 2.2 and ‘adversarial robustness inherited with noise modeling’ in Appendix D. For each of these cases, inherit means ‘accounts for’ or ‘incorporates’. Similarly, ‘inculcate’ has also been used in such context.

d.	‘right prediction vs right explanation’: The term ‘explainable’ was used in the context that noise (on account of being trained with the model) discovers some knowledge about the input/output distribution. We did not mean to confuse with interpretability of a network’s decision making procedure . Here, we wanted to imply that noise modeling helps a model to not only predict correctly (with comparable test accuracy on clean data as standard SGD training) but also incorporate more knowledge about out-of-sample data (i.e. adversarial inputs) yielding robustness.

2)	"off manifold" is used often but is highly vague. 
In our introduction, we have mentioned citing [R1] that ‘adversarial examples (off manifold misclassified points) occur in close proximity to randomly chosen inputs on the data manifold that are, in fact, correctly classified’. On-manifold data refers to clean data points while off-manifold to adversarial points. We explicitly say that ‘we hypothesize that the model learns to look in the vicinity of the on-manifold data points and thereby incorporate more out-of-sample data (without using any direct data augmentation) that, in turn, improves its’ generalization capability in the off-manifold input space’. Furthermore, our PCA results in Section2.3 are dedicated towards validating the hypothesis that the noise training does in fact have an effect on the behavior of the model when analysed with adversarial and clean data. Also, our PC variance and distance analysis, as well as, the adversarial subspace dimensionality do empirically justify that models trained with ExL (or in fact explicit adversarial training) incorporate off-manifold (or adversarial data) points. This is seen with higher variance, lower PC cosine distance and reduced number of adversarial dimensions.
To summarize, we have used the term off-manifold data introduced in [R1] to refer to adversarial data and justify that ExL does in fact embrace off-manifold data points with our PCA analysis.
[R1] Gilmer, Justin, et al. "Adversarial spheres." arXiv preprint arXiv:1801.02774 (2018).

content.title: Response to Reviewer2 (Part2)
content.comment:
Clarity Related:
3)	Likelihood section is deemed highly vague.
In Section 2.2, we have presented a general optimization perspective from a maximum likelihood criterion to give an idea of adversarial robustness. We have explicitly mentioned that X represents the on-manifold data points and A is the off-manifold adversarial data points. In adversarial training methods, we augment the training dataset with adversarial inputs while maximizing the criterion p(Y|X, A)  where the model tries to maximize the probability of Y given samples that belong to X as well as A. Model that maximizes p(Y|X) is susceptible to adversarial attacks since it does not have knowledge of adversarial data A. We have presented a basic intuition as how the model behaves by presenting this likelihood criterion. We wanted to give our readers an idea as to how including N and doing noise training can have some sort of a generative behavior. This is meant to provide intuition and context about adversarial robustness from a discriminative and generative viewpoint. We have used terms like ‘we believe the partial and implicit generative modeling behavior imparts a model trained with ExL more knowledge about both on and off-manifold data points’. Coming up with a theoretical background justifying such perspective is not the motive of this paper. We ourselves do not know how to put this implicit modeling into a theoretical perspective justifying the robustness that we achieve. This is the reason why we used PCA analysis to justify that there is some interesting behavior we observe with PC variance and distance that is in coherence with ExL as well as adversarial training methods.

Quality Related:
1)	Fixing noise across batch:
Since we are training the noise, we need to reuse the noise maps across different mini-batches. We want to make sure that the characteristics of noise learnt in 1st iteration are preserved and passed onto the 2nd iteration of training. This will help the noise, fed to the network with the input (X*N), to enable the overall loss minimization procedure during training. If we introduce new N for each iteration, there will not be any learning of noise. This is equivalent to introducing randomly perturbation every iteration and the noise will not inherit any characteristics. 
On that point, introducing random noise at each iteration is equivalent to perturbing examples during training. This is a way for making the network robust to external perturbations (different from adversarial perturbation). This helps in improving a network’s generalization capability. However, as shown in [R1, R2], using random noise during training does not help adversarial robustness.
Our choice was based on empirical observation and an intuition that for the noise to actually learn something we need to reuse the maps across different iterations during training. We do not have any theoretical backups to support this choice, at present, except for experimental evaluation (that shows successful results) and intuition. 
[R1] Fawzi, Alhussein, Seyed-Mohsen Moosavi-Dezfooli, and Pascal Frossard. "Robustness of classifiers: from adversarial to random noise." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. 2016.
[R2] Goodfellow, Ian J, Shlens, Jonathon, and Szegedy, Christian. Explaining and harnessing adversarial examples. In Proc. ICLR, 2015.

content.title: Response to Reviewer2 (Part3)
content.comment:
Quality Related:
2)	Excessive linearity & off-manifold data –context and comments
Several prior works have hypothesized the susceptibility of ML models to adversarial attacks due to the overly linear behavior of deep neural models in a high dimensional input space [R1-R2]. Similarly, ‘adversarial examples are off the data manifold’ is a phrase mentioned and explained in prior works [R3-R4]. They say that training data points are on-manifold data and since the model only generalizes on on-manifold data points, it falls susceptible to off-manifold points where the network’s behavior becomes overly linear. We have explicitly given the context of off-manifold data as adversarial data in the Introduction and present our opinion on why a model fails against adversarial attacks, drawing conclusion from the prior work’s analysis and results. We say that ‘Combining the two, we infer that excessive linearity causes models to extrapolate their behavior beyond the data manifold yielding pathological results for slightly perturbed inputs.’ Here ‘two’ refers to the two facts already known about adversarial susceptibility: overly linear behavior and adversarial data being off-manifold data.

To that effect, our PCA results and accuracy results show that ExL noise modeling improves the robustness of a model than standard SGD. This empirical result points to the fact that noise modeling might in fact incorporate some adversarial data points during training while helping a model to generalize its behavior in the off-manifold data space. As mentioned earlier, we rely on empirical results to validate our hypothesis. If the reviewer is concerned with theoretical backups, we, unfortunately, do not have such expertise. Having said that, the presented PCA analysis provides justification for how adversarial training, in general, and ExL, to be specific, do improve the robustness of a model by having a marked difference in the variance and cosine distance behavior. Furthermore, our PCA analysis lets us peek into a model’s behavior since we are analyzing the intermediate layer’s activations to see such results.

Finally, we do understand the reviewer’s concerns about clarity in term usage. We can modify the paper and explicate certain meaning. However, we would like to mention hat off-manifold, out-of-sample terms have been introduced in earlier works. We take that and put it in our context. While we do not have rigorous theoretical backups, we think the PCA analysis presents a very interesting and informative behavior on not only ExL training but also adversarial training that can used to evaluate adversarial robustness in general context.
[R1] Goodfellow, Ian J, Shlens, Jonathon, and Szegedy, Christian. Explaining and harnessing adversarial examples. In Proc. ICLR, 2015.
[R2] Luo, Yan, et al. "Foveation-based mechanisms alleviate adversarial examples." arXiv preprint arXiv:1511.06292(2015).
[R3] Lee, Hyeungill, Sungyeob Han, and Jungwoo Lee. "Generative Adversarial Trainer: Defense to Adversarial Perturbations with GAN." arXiv preprint arXiv:1705.03387(2017).
[R4] Gilmer, Justin, et al. "Adversarial spheres." arXiv preprint arXiv:1801.02774 (2018).

display_title: Potentially interesting ideas but exposition and motivation are too imprecise

content.title: Potentially interesting ideas but exposition and motivation are too imprecise
content.review:
The authors suggest a novel approach, ExL to adversial training using multiplicate noise that is learned jointly with model parameters using SGD. They propose a likelihood framework to interpret why the approach is successful. PCA of intermediate layers is used to suggest that ExL trained NNs are more robust because they better cover space around the observed data manifold. Results on three canonical datasets using blackbox and whitebox adversarial attacks suggest that ExL can be helpful in defending against BB attacks, and is easily combined with other adversial training approaches such as PGD to further improve robustness. 

I think there are some interesting ideas in the paper but the motivation is too hand-wavey and the method exposition is insufficient. Firstly, refering to N as "noise" seems problematic. N is learned so is more akin to a latent variable than noise. In particular it is not random at any point apart from initialization (which is equally true for model parameters). Additionally it is very strange to me that these "learned masks" are fixed in position in the mini-batch, since an index in the minibatch has no external meaning. The authors don't say whether the data points are permuted at each epoch, which is important since it effects whether the same data point at subsequent epochs uses the same mask (I don't even know from the exposition whether this is intended or not). 

Secondly, the "likelihood framework" is very hand-wavey. When modeling P(Y|X) we think of Y and X as random variables, with the training set (X_train, Y_train) as samples. Nothing in this says that P(Y|X) should not hold for X other than X_train, e.g. X=A. Thus the introduction of P(Y|X,A) is superfluous. While Eq 1 is mathematically correct it is therefore pretty meaningless in terms of understanding what ExL is doing. The text does little to help. 

Thirdly, "Explainable" in the title is dangerously close to "interpretable", which ExL is certainly not. The N give only the vaguest sense of the features being used in the data (see Fig 1b). 

There might be Bayesian/likelihood-based interpretation of ExL, other than that proposed by the authors. I was surprised the similarity to dropout wasn't mentioned. Yarin Gal's work pointed out the similarity between dropout and variational Bayes with a specific variational posterior, and the ExL looks a look like opitmizing the resulting objective including per pixel dropout weights (although not stochastically which is strange). Alternatively one could think of X*N as latent variables and we are modeling P(Y|X*N). This could be interpreted as modeling noise in X for example. 

The connection to dropout makes me suspicious that while ExL is proposed as an adversarial training method it is really just performing more effective regularization, which should in itself smooth the prediciton surface and improve robustness to adversarial examples. It would be feasible to test this, for example by comparing different formes of regularization with and without ExL. 

Why threshold grad L < 0 when learning N? What stops the model from just setting N=0? 

Minor comments
- Abstact: "prove" -> "show" (proofs require proofs!)
- Don't re-use N as the number of training images. 
- page 5. X=X+alpha... ugh.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

replying_to: Replying to Potentially interesting ideas but exposition and motivation are too imprecise

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1 (Part1)
content.comment:
1)	Regarding permutation of data points at each epoch

We do not permute the data points at each epoch. Hence, the learnt mask corresponding to a data point in one epoch is in fact reused by the same data point in the next epoch. Further, during inference, we use the mean of the ‘learnt noise maps’ and pass it with the input to get a prediction. Using latent variable terminology instead of noise is a helpful suggestion. 

2)	Likelihood framework- handwavey.

In Section 2.2, we have presented a general optimization perspective from a maximum likelihood criterion to give an idea of adversarial robustness. We have explicitly mentioned that X represents the on-manifold data points (i.e. training samples X_data) and A is the off-manifold adversarial data points. In adversarial training methods, we augment the training dataset with adversarial inputs while maximizing the criterion p(Y|X, A),  where the model tries to maximize the probability of Y given samples that belong to X as well as A. Here, we wanted to point out that given the joint distribution  of (X,A), the model maximized the probability of Y, looking at both on and off-manifold data with adversarial training. Model that maximizes p(Y|X) is susceptible to adversarial attacks since it does not have knowledge of adversarial data A. 

We have presented a basic intuition as how the model behaves by presenting this likelihood criterion. We wanted to give our readers an idea as to how including N and doing noise training can have some sort of a generative behavior. This is meant to provide intuition and context about adversarial robustness from a discriminative and generative viewpoint. We have used terms like ‘we believe the partial and implicit generative modeling behavior imparts a model trained with ExL more knowledge about both on and off-manifold data points’. Coming up with a theoretical background justifying such perspective is not the motive of this paper. We ourselves do not know how to put this implicit modeling into a theoretical perspective justifying the robustness that we achieve. This is the reason why we used PCA analysis to justify that there is some interesting behavior we observe with PC variance and distance that is in coherence with ExL as well as adversarial training methods.

3)	The term ‘explainable’ was used in the context that noise (on account of being trained with the model) discovers some knowledge about the input/output distribution. We did not mean to confuse with interpretability of a network’s decision making procedure. We will change the title of the paper to “Implicit Generative Modeling of Random Noise during Training for Adversarial Robustness”. 

4)	Similarity of dropout and variational Bayes

We do think that the fact that noise introduced is multiplicative in nature has some resemblance to dropout like regularization which is a multiplicative stochastic property. We do not have precise theoretical analysis to currently present a backup of why ExL and P(Y|X*N) modeling actually provides adversarial robustness. However, ExL noise might be optimizing the objective function similar to pixel dropout weights. Since the noise is learnt, we think that the per pixel dropout weight probability is something that might be getting learnt with the noise masks.

content.title: Response to Reviewer1 (Part2)
content.comment:
5)	ExL performing regularization

We do agree with the reviewer’s intuition that ExL is performing some sort of regularization thereby  enhancing the model’s generalization capability on adversarial data points. In fact, the smoothening of the loss surface curves in Fig. 5 also point to this. We would like to further point out that adversarial training [R1, R2] (where adversarial data points are augmented in the training dataset) is also a form of regularization that improves adversarial robustness. Hence, adversarial data augmentation also is a more effective regularization technique. As far as ExL is concerned, the current comparison between ExL and SGD in table 1/2 incorporated weight decay regularization (in both SGD, ExL) which shows that ExL performs better with higher adversarial accuracy. We also compared 4 scenarios: ExL(with explicit dropout), ExL(without dropout), SGD(with dropout) and SGD (without dropout) and see that adversarial accuracy against BB attacks is much higher with ExL training (~20% higher than SGD on MNIST with PGD-40 attacks). The accuracy follows the order: ExL (with explicit dropout)> ExL (without dropout)> SGD (with dropout)> SGD (without dropout). 
While ExL like adversarial training is an effective regularization technique, the fact that it improves adversarial robustness is a significant result.
[R1] Madry, Aleksander, et al. "Towards deep learning models resistant to adversarial attacks." arXiv preprint arXiv:1706.06083 (2017).
[R2] Tramèr, Florian, et al. "Ensemble adversarial training: Attacks and defenses." arXiv preprint arXiv:1705.07204 (2017).

6)	Grad(L_N)<0:
In our experiments, we found out that using only negative gradient for the noise masks (i.e. Grad(Loss_N)) during backpropagation yields best accuracy closer to that of standard SGD model. Since, we did not want to compromise on clean accuracy with ExL training, we chose to use negative gradients only for learning noise (not for paarmeters, theta) while performing model training. We have justified this Fig. 2 of the paper. Since it is multiplicative noise (X*N), and noise inherently takes part  in the overall loss minimization procedure, if the model sets N=0, the input will be 0 (since X*N). This will cause the loss to rise thereby having a counter productive effect on training. The fact that noise takes part in the model’s loss minimization (while being trained) lets the noise to incorporate some characteristics about the input as well as model’s behavior such that overall loss in the predictive pathway is minimized. Having said that, this is our intuition on how and why noise modeling helps. Looking at the trained noise maps, we also see that noise always learns some interesting behavior that in turn helps the model during training (and overall loss minimization)

7)	Minor comments
a.	Prove justification: We have said in the abstract that ‘We prove our approach's efficacy and provide a simplistic visualization tool for understanding adversarial data, using Principal Component Analysis.’ To reiterate, we have used prove in the context of PCA to say that our PCA result do prove the approach’s efficacy. Since we have provided PCA variance and distance results that do suggest ExL trained models are more robust, the use of prove seems appropriate.
b.	N as number of training images was used to explain the summation upper limit N used in PCA. We can change this to avoid confusion.
c.	page 5. X=X+alpha... ugh.
In Page 5, we have used X+alpha *sign(…) to explain the random-step FGSM attack metric. We have notified that alpha = epsilon/2 where epsilon is the perturbation level. We understand it can be frustrating to review so many papers and find minor errors. If you could please clarify what you meant to be clarified by this comment, we will really appreciate it.

replying_to: Replying to Explainable Adversarial Learning: Implicit Generative Modeling of Random Noise during Training for Adversarial Robustness

content.title: Submission Withdrawn by the Authors
content.withdrawal confirmation: I have read and agree with the withdrawal statement on behalf of myself and my co-authors.
